entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen21913" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21914" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21915" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21914" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> All nations are exhorted to praise the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.1">Psa 100:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.2">Psa 100:2</reference>; to acknowledge him to be the Sovereign God and their Creator and that they are his people and the flock of his pasture, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>; to worship him publicly, and be grateful for his mercies, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.4">Psa 100:4</reference>. The reasons on which this is founded; his own goodness, his everlasting mercy, and his ever-during truth, <reference osisRef="Psa.100.5">Psa 100:5</reference>. <div eID="gen21916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21917" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is entitled in the Hebrew מזמור לתודה mizmor lethodah, not "A Psalm of Praise," as we have it, but "A Psalm for the confession, or for the confession-offering," very properly translated by the Chaldee: שבחא על קורבן תודתא shibcha al kurban todetha, "Praise for the sacrifice (or offering) of confession." The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Ethiopic have followed this sense. The Arabic attributes it to David. The Syriac has the following prefixed: "Without a name. Concerning Joshua the son of Nun, when he had ended the war with the Ammonites: but in the new covenant it relates to the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith." It is likely that it was composed after the captivity, as a form of thanksgiving to God for that great deliverance, as well as an inducement to the people to consecrate themselves to him, and to be exact in the performance of the acts of public worship. <div eID="gen21917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21918" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> Make a joyful noise - הריעו hariu, exult, triumph, leap for joy. <div eID="gen21919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> All ye lands - Not only Jews, but Gentiles, for the Lord bestows his benefits on all with a liberal hand.

The reasons on which this is founded; his own goodness, his everlasting mercy, and his ever-during truth, Psa 100:5 . Concerning Joshua the son of Nun, when he had ended the war with the Ammonites: but in the new covenant it relates to the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith." entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21921" type="x-p"/> Serve the Lord with gladness - It is your privilege and duty to be happy in your religious worship. The religion of the true God is intended to remove human misery, and to make mankind happy. He whom the religion of Christ has not made happy does not understand that religion, or does not make a proper use of it.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21922" type="x-p"/> Know ye that the Lord he is God - Acknowledge in every possible way, both in public and private, that Jehovah, the uncreated self-existent, and eternal Being, is Elohim, the God who is in covenant with man, to instruct, redeem, love, and make him finally happy. <div eID="gen21922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21923" type="x-p"/> It is he that hath made us - He is our Creator and has consequently the only right in and over us. <div eID="gen21923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21924" type="x-p"/> And not we ourselves - ולא אנחנו velo anachnu. I can never think that this is the true reading, though found in the present Hebrew text, in the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Syriac. Was there ever a people on earth, however grossly heathenish, that did believe, or could believe, that they had made themselves? In twenty-six of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. we have ולו אנחנו velo anachnu, "and His we are;" לו lo, the pronoun, being put for לא lo, the negative particle. This is the reading of the Targum, or Chaldee paraphrase ודיליה אנחנא vedileyh anachna, "and his we are," and is the reading of the text in the Complutensian Polyglot, of both the Psalters which were printed in 1477, and is the keri, or marginal reading in most Masoretic Bibles. Every person must see, from the nature of the subject that it is the genuine reading. The position is founded on the maxim that what a man invents, constructs out of his own matterials, without assistance in genius, materials or execution from any other person, is His Own and to it, its use, and produce, he has the only right. God made us, therefore we are His: we are his people, and should acknowledge him for our God; we are the sheep of his pasture, and should devote the lives to him constantly which he continually supports.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21925" type="x-p"/> Enter into his gates with thanksgiving - Publicly worship God; and when ye come to the house of prayer, be thankful that you have such a privilege; and when you enter his courts, praise him for the permission. <div eID="gen21925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21926" type="x-p"/> The word בתודה bethodah, which we render with thanksgiving, is properly with the confession-offering or sacrifice. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.100.1-Psa.100.5">Psa 100:1-5</reference> (note). <div eID="gen21926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21927" type="x-p"/> Bless his name - Bless Jehovah, that he is your Elohim; see <reference osisRef="Psa.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference>. In our liturgic service we say, "Speak good of his name;" we cannot do otherwise; we have nothing but good to speak of our God.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21928" type="x-p"/> For the Lord is good - Goodness the perfect, eternal opposition to all badness and evil, is essential to God. Mercy and compassion are modifications of his goodness; and as his nature is eternal, so his mercy, springing from his goodness, must be everlasting. And as Truth is an essential characteristic of an infinitely intelligent and perfect nature; therefore God's truth must endure from generation to generation. Whatsoever he has promised must be fulfilled, through all the successive generations of men, as long as sun and moon shall last. <div eID="gen21928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21929" type="x-p"/> As this is a very important Psalm, and has long made a part of our public worship, I shall lay it before the reader in the oldest vernacular Versions I have hitherto met with, - the Anglo-Saxon and the Anglo-Scottish, with a literal interlineary translation of the former. <div eID="gen21929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21930" type="x-p"/> The Anglo-Saxon Hundredth Psalm <div eID="gen21930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21931" type="x-p"/> Rhyme ye the Lord all earth, serve the Lord in bliss; <div eID="gen21931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21932" type="x-p"/> Infare in sight his in blithness; <div eID="gen21932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21933" type="x-p"/> Wit ye, for that Lord he is God, he did us &not self we; <div eID="gen21933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21934" type="x-p"/> Folk his &sheep leeseway his; fare into gates his in confession, into courts is in hymns confess him. <div eID="gen21934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21935" type="x-p"/> Praise name his, for that winsom is; Lord thro' eternity mildheartedness his, &unto on kindred &kindred sothfastnes his <div eID="gen21935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21936" type="x-p"/> The reader will see that, in order to make this translation as literal as possible, I have preserved some old English words which we had from the Anglo-Saxon, and which have nearly become obsolete: e.g., Infare, "to go in;" blithness, "joy, exultation;" twit ye, "know ye;" did, the preterite of to do, "made, created," the literal translation of the Hebrew, עשה asah, he made; leeseway, "pasturage on a common;" winsom, "cheerful, merry;" mildheartedness, "tenderness of heart, compassion;" sothfastness, "steady to the sooth or truth, fast to truth." I might have noticed some various readings in Anglo-Saxon MSS.; e.g., <reference osisRef="Psa.100.1">Psa 100:1</reference> for idrymeth, "rhyme ye;" winsumiath, "be winsom, be joyful." And <reference osisRef="Psa.100.5">Psa 100:5</reference>, for winsom, "cheerful;" swete, "sweet." <div eID="gen21936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21937" type="x-p"/> Anglo-Scottish Version of the Hundredth Psalm <div eID="gen21937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21938" type="x-p"/> 1. Enters in his sight with joying. <div eID="gen21939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21940" type="x-p"/> 3. Wittes for Lorde he is God; he made us and noght we; <div eID="gen21940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21941" type="x-p"/> 4. Folke of hym, and schepe of his pasture; enters the gates of hym in schrift; hys Halles in ympnys; schryves to hym. <div eID="gen21941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21942" type="x-p"/> 5. Loues his name, for soft is Lorde; withouten end in his mercy; and in generation and generation the sothfastnes of hym. <div eID="gen21942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21943" type="x-p"/> Thus our forefathers said and sung in heart and mouth and with their tongues made confession to salvation. entries.content_plain: Verse 5 For the Lord is good - Goodness the perfect, eternal opposition to all badness and evil, is essential to God. Mercy and compassion are modifications of his goodness; and as his nature is eternal, so his mercy, springing from his goodness, must be everlasting. And as Truth is an essential characteristic of an infinitely intelligent and perfect nature; therefore God's truth must endure from generation to generation. Whatsoever he has promised must be fulfilled, through all the successive generations of men, as long as sun and moon shall last. As this is a very important Psalm, and has long made a part of our public worship, I shall lay it before the reader in the oldest vernacular Versions I have hitherto met with, - the Anglo-Saxon and the Anglo-Scottish, with a literal interlineary translation of the former. The Anglo-Saxon Hundredth Psalm Rhyme ye the Lord all earth, serve the Lord in bliss; Infare in sight his in blithness; Wit ye, for that Lord he is God, he did us ¬ self we; Folk his &sheep leeseway his; fare into gates his in confession, into courts is in hymns confess him. Praise name his, for that winsom is; Lord thro' eternity mildheartedness his, &unto on kindred &kindred sothfastnes his The reader will see that, in order to make this translation as literal as possible, I have preserved some old English words which we had from the Anglo-Saxon, and which have nearly become obsolete: e.g., Infare, "to go in;" blithness, "joy, exultation;" twit ye, "know ye;" did, the preterite of to do, "made, created," the literal translation of the Hebrew, עשה asah, he made; leeseway, "pasturage on a common;" winsom, "cheerful, merry;" mildheartedness, "tenderness of heart, compassion;" sothfastness, "steady to the sooth or truth, fast to truth." I might have noticed some various readings in Anglo-Saxon MSS.; e.g., Psa 100:1 for idrymeth, "rhyme ye;" winsumiath, "be winsom, be joyful." And Psa 100:5 , for winsom, "cheerful;" swete, "sweet." Anglo-Scottish Version of the Hundredth Psalm 1. Joyes to God al the erth; serves to Lord in gladnes. 2. Enters in his sight with joying. 3. Wittes for Lorde he is God; he made us and noght we; 4. Folke of hym, and schepe of his pasture; enters the gates of hym in schrift; hys Halles in ympnys; schryves to hym. 5. Loues his name, for soft is Lorde; withouten end in his mercy; and in generation and generation the sothfastnes of hym. Thus our forefathers said and sung in heart and mouth and with their tongues made confession to salvation. There are but few words here which require explanation: Psa 100:3 , Wittes, "wot ye, know ye." Psa 100:4 , Schrift, "confession;" schryves, "confess ye." Verse 6 , Loues, "praise ye, laud ye." Sothfastness, as above, steadfastness in the truth.
